section_summary: This section is dominated by public, clerical, academic, missionary, and congressional protests against American exports of arms, aircraft, petroleum, iron, steel, scrap, and other war materials to Japan during the Sino-Japanese War. State Department replies repeatedly explain that the Neutrality Act could not be applied unless the President formally proclaimed a state of war, that it would then restrict trade with both China and Japan, and that existing law did not authorize embargoes on commodities such as oil or scrap iron. The section also contains cross-reference sheets on proposed international sanctions, petitions from church congregations, and vivid missionary testimony about Japanese bombing casualties at Hankow and Wuchang.

subfiles.title: Continuation of State Department reply explaining the Neutrality Act
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Continues an explanation of why the administration had not invoked the Neutrality Act against China and Japan.
subfiles.summary: Reply continuation: a presidential war proclamation would bar arms and long-term credits to both China and Japan, none is legally available without it, the President judged invocation contrary to broader interests, and license values are reported.

subfiles.title: Frank M. Silsley to Cordell Hull urging an end to shipments to Japan
subfiles.about: Urges the State Department to stop shipments of arms and war materials that allegedly sustain Japan's invasion of China.
subfiles.summary: Frank Silsley argues American arms and long-term credits make the U.S. morally complicit in Japanese aggression, appealing to idealism and Christian duty, citing millions of Chinese refugees.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Frank M. Silsley
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Explains the legal and policy reasons for not applying the Neutrality Act to the Sino-Japanese conflict.
subfiles.summary: Yost tells Silsley the act would bar exports and long-term credits to both countries only after a presidential war finding, ordinary commodities aren't covered, and invocation was judged not in U.S. interest; resolution, pamphlet and license totals enclosed.

subfiles.title: Frederick B. Stewart transmits a church resolution
subfiles.about: Transmits a unanimously approved letter from the Washington Park Methodist Episcopal Church Quarterly Conference.
subfiles.summary: Frederick Stewart forwards a church conference resolution on American support for the Far Eastern war to the Secretary of State.

subfiles.title: Washington Park Methodist Episcopal Church appeal against war-sustaining trade
subfiles.from: Secretary, Washington Park Methodist Episcopal Church Quarterly Conference
subfiles.about: Calls upon Hull to end American trade sustaining the war against China.
subfiles.summary: Washington Park Methodist Episcopal Church conference says war-sustaining traffic makes the U.S. a partner in the Far Eastern conflict and asks Hull to act against it.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Frederick B. Stewart
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Responds to the Washington Park church appeal with the Department's standard Neutrality Act explanation.
subfiles.summary: The reply explains that an arms embargo would apply to both China and Japan only following a presidential war proclamation. It says the President did not consider invocation in the national interest and that non-arms commodities could not be prohibited under the act. Export-license figures and enclosures are provided.

subfiles.title: D. Brewer Eddy protests exports to Japan
subfiles.about: Protests American exports of munitions, gasoline, steel, and iron products to Japan.
subfiles.summary: D. Brewer Eddy endorses the pamphlet "America's Share in Japan's War Guilt," calls trade with Japan a moral failure, and reports strong public support for firmer policy.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to D. Brewer Eddy
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Explains why the government could not prohibit arms or strategic-material exports to Japan under existing law.
subfiles.summary: Yost tells Eddy the act needs a presidential proclamation and would hit both belligerents; gasoline, steel and iron weren't in the statutory arms list, so no authority exists to prohibit them; license totals given.

subfiles.title: Evarts G. Loomis protests a Japanese freighter's cargo
subfiles.about: Reports seeing a Japanese ship loaded at Brooklyn with aircraft motors, trucks, steel, and alleged shrapnel and demands immediate action.
subfiles.summary: Evarts Loomis condemns Americans for supplying much of Japan's war equipment in China, calls the profits tainted, and asks the government to remove the stain.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Evarts G. Loomis
subfiles.about: Answers Loomis's protest by outlining the limits of the Neutrality Act and the administration's opposition to civilian bombing.
subfiles.summary: Yost tells Loomis an embargo needs a presidential proclamation and would cover China and Japan, ordinary goods are outside the act; license totals cited, and the government's bombing condemnation was communicated to manufacturers.

subfiles.title: Homer H. Dubs urges termination of military trade with Japan
subfiles.about: Urges the United States to stop supplying Japan with goods usable for military purposes.
subfiles.summary: Homer Dubs is ashamed the U.S. assists Japan despite broad condemnation, arguing the trade earned Japanese contempt and weakened American prestige.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Homer H. Dubs
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Provides the Department's standard response concerning the Neutrality Act and arms exports.
subfiles.summary: State says it can't single out Japan without a formal war finding, which would embargo China too; invocation was judged contrary to U.S. interests, non-arms goods are beyond the act, and license figures are included.

subfiles.title: Brownell Gage praises Hull and requests action against exports to Japan
subfiles.about: Praises Hull's denunciation of aggressive force and asks him to prevent American participation in Japanese aggression.
subfiles.summary: Brownell Gage cites Hull's June 3 Nashville address condemning aggression and asks the administration to stop munitions and raw-material sales making the U.S. a partner in Japan's war.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Brownell Gage
subfiles.about: Thanks Gage for supporting Hull's speeches and explains why the Neutrality Act had not been invoked.
subfiles.summary: State welcomes Gage's support but repeats that a war finding would embargo China and Japan, invocation was judged inconsistent with U.S. interests, and the act can't regulate commodities beyond the arms list; license figures supplied.

subfiles.title: James M. Yard renews request to apply the Neutrality Law
subfiles.about: Argues that the Neutrality Law should be applied despite its effect on both China and Japan.
subfiles.summary: James Yard renews his request to apply the Neutrality Law, granting technical difficulties and that more war materials went to China, but calling Japan the aggressor and saying Chinese officials would welcome it.

subfiles.title: Augustine Lonergan forwards Mrs. Parsons's protest
subfiles.about: Forwards a constituent's letter urging an end to war-supply exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Senator Lonergan refers Mrs. Edgerton Parsons's letter to the Department and keeps a copy.

subfiles.title: Mrs. Edgerton Parsons urges an embargo on Japan
subfiles.about: Endorses action to halt American munitions and war supplies to Japan while its invasion of China continues.
subfiles.summary: Mrs. Parsons asks Senator Lonergan to help secure government and popular action against exports to Japan for the duration of the invasion.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Mrs. Edgerton Parsons
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Green, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Responds to Parsons's embargo request with a legal explanation and a statement condemning civilian bombing.
subfiles.summary: Green tells Mrs. Parsons a Neutrality Act embargo needs a war proclamation and would apply equally to China and Japan, broader commodities can't be prohibited, license totals given, and the government has urged aircraft makers not to encourage attacks on civilians.

subfiles.title: Sumner Welles replies to Senator Lonergan
subfiles.about: Acknowledges Lonergan's referral and encloses the Department's response to Mrs. Parsons.
subfiles.summary: Welles confirms receipt of Lonergan's letter and the constituent protest and sends a copy of the reply to Mrs. Parsons.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Irwin H. Linton report
subfiles.about: Directs researchers to a report from a U.S. missionary in China about Japanese atrocities and arms sales.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: Irwin Linton's report on Japanese atrocities recommending ending arms sales to Japan, filed elsewhere.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Koo's Geneva embargo speech
subfiles.about: References a telegram reporting Koo's League Assembly speech recommending broad sanctions against Japan.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: Koo's Geneva Assembly speech calling for an embargo on arms, aircraft, oil, raw materials and credits.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Chinese embargo proposal in the League's Third Committee
subfiles.about: References a telegram reporting a Chinese request for an embargo on military aircraft and oil exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: Chinese delegate urged the League's Third Committee to embargo military planes and oil for Japan, per a Disarmament Conference telegram.

subfiles.title: Charles L. McNary refers the Carpenters' protest
subfiles.about: Requests State Department comments on an Oregon couple's protest against munitions traffic to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Senator McNary says Leonard Carpenter and his wife oppose munitions shipments to Japan and asks the Department's views.

subfiles.title: Sumner Welles replies to Senator McNary
subfiles.about: Provides materials and suggested language for McNary's response to the Carpenters.
subfiles.summary: Welles suggests sending the Carpenters the Joint Resolution and "International Traffic in Arms"; a proclamation would embargo both sides, non-arms goods are outside the act, and the President judged invocation not in the broader interest.

subfiles.title: Pasadena Presbyterian Church petition sent through William G. McAdoo
subfiles.from: Dr. Freeman and members of Pasadena Presbyterian Church
subfiles.to: William G. McAdoo, for the President
subfiles.about: Petitions the President to end American trade assisting Japan's destruction of China.
subfiles.summary: The petitioners condemn Japanese attacks on noncombatants and state that American aircraft and munitions aid the aggressor. Invoking the Good Neighbor policy, they ask the President to place moral standards above financial interests. Two additional pages contain numerous congregational signatures.

subfiles.title: State Department acknowledgment to Dr. Freeman
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Acknowledges the McAdoo-transmitted petition and points Freeman to an earlier substantive reply.
subfiles.summary: At Senator McAdoo's request Yost acknowledges Dr. Freeman's September 18 petition and refers him to the Department's October 6 response.

subfiles.title: Missionary-society resolution sent to President Roosevelt
subfiles.from: David J. Fant, for the Board of Managers
subfiles.about: Transmits a unanimous resolution demanding an end to American material support for Japanese aggression.
subfiles.summary: Missionary-society resolution cites Japan's alleged Nine-Power Treaty and Kellogg Pact violations, condemns attacks on cities, expresses shame at American supplies, and, for 500-plus churches, asks Roosevelt to end the traffic.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to David J. Fant
subfiles.about: Acknowledges the missionary resolution and explains the administration's legal position on trade with Japan.
subfiles.summary: Yost thanks David Fant, repeating the act works only after a presidential war finding and then against both combatants, ordinary goods aren't covered, license totals and the bombing condemnation included.

subfiles.title: William G. Owens argues against supplying Japan
subfiles.about: Uses his experience in Shanghai to argue that the United States should stop exports usable in Japan's war.
subfiles.summary: William Owens recalls Japan's manufactured Shanghai incident and munitions-independence claims, argues supplying munitions, cotton, iron and oil violates moral and commercial interests, and warns a conquered China could become another Manchukuo.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to William G. Owens
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Answers Owens's objections with the Department's legal interpretation of the Neutrality Act.
subfiles.summary: State tells Owens an embargo follows only a presidential war finding and would apply to both countries, invocation was judged contrary to U.S. interests, and other commodities aren't covered; totals, resolution and pamphlet enclosed.

subfiles.title: Lillian Picken appeals to Roosevelt from India
subfiles.about: Urges legislation prohibiting exports of arms and all war materials to Japan and other aggressor nations.
subfiles.summary: Lillian Picken, a missionary in India, says American bombs help slaughter Chinese noncombatants and asks Roosevelt to lead the nation in accepting an effective embargo's sacrifices; she encloses a nurse's account.

subfiles.title: Gladys Stephenson's Hankow letter with Florence E. Schafer's circulation appeal
subfiles.to: Florence E. Schafer; friends and prospective protesters
subfiles.about: Describes bombing casualties around Hankow and Wuchang and asks Americans to protest sales of war materials to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Gladys Stephenson describes civilians killed in Japanese raids near Hankow and Wuchang and bomb parts from the U.S. and Britain; Florence Schafer's August 24 note from Kolhapur urges recipients to press Washington to end U.S. participation.

subfiles.title: Instructions to the American Consular Officer at Bombay concerning Picken and Schafer
subfiles.to: American Consular Officer in charge, Bombay
subfiles.about: Directs the consular officer to answer the two missionaries using the Department's standard explanation and enclosures.
subfiles.summary: Instruction to the Bombay consular officer forwards the Picken and Schafer correspondence and Stephenson's Hankow letter, suggesting he explain the Neutrality Act needs a proclamation, would hit both China and Japan, and wasn't invoked; arms figures and Hull's bombing condemnation are included.

subfiles.title: Mrs. Sherrod protests exports of war materials to Japan
subfiles.about: Protests American exports, including oil, scrap iron, and steel, that could support Japan's war effort.
subfiles.summary: Severely damaged protest by Mrs. Sherrod, identified from the reply, on war-material exports to Japan including arms, oil, scrap and steel.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Mrs. Sherrod
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Explains that existing law did not authorize an embargo on oil, scrap iron, or steel.
subfiles.summary: State tells Mrs. Sherrod the Neutrality Act needs a presidential war proclamation and would restrict both China and Japan; oil, scrap iron and steel aren't defined arms, so no statute lets the President or Secretary prohibit them.

subfiles.title: Walter G. Hiltner denounces exports and European appeasement
subfiles.about: Calls for action against shipments to Japan and condemns the treatment of Czechoslovakia by European leaders.
subfiles.summary: Walter Hiltner calls munitions, machinery and raw-material exports to Japan a national disgrace, urges withholding loans and nonrecognition of seized territory, and condemns British and French concessions to Germany at Czechoslovakia's expense.

subfiles.title: State Department acknowledgment to Walter G. Hiltner
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Acknowledges Hiltner's letter and refers him to an earlier Department response.
subfiles.summary: Yost acknowledges Hiltner's further letter on the Far East and refers him to the October 1 reply.

subfiles.title: Ann Arbor correspondent criticizes American neutrality
subfiles.about: Rejects the Department's defense of equal treatment for China and Japan and advocates boycotts of aggressor states.
subfiles.summary: Ann Arbor writer cites The Nation's "Partnership with Japan," calls equal supply to aggressor and victim indefensible neutrality, urges boycotting Japan, Germany and Italy, and says policy ignores public opinion.

subfiles.title: Maude Scritchfield protests a San Diego scrap-iron shipment
subfiles.about: Protests repeated scrap-iron exports from San Diego to Japan and encloses a report of a planned 4,000-ton shipment.
subfiles.summary: Maude Scritchfield sends a San Diego Union clipping on 4,000 tons of scrap shipped from Pier 1 to Osaka, notes many earlier cargoes, and asks attention for the Federation of State Societies' protest.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Maude Scritchfield
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Explains that scrap iron was excluded from the Neutrality Act's restricted categories.
subfiles.summary: Yost states that the act authorized restrictions on defined arms, ammunition, and implements of war in specified conflicts. Because scrap iron and similar products were expressly outside those categories, no statute then empowered the President to prohibit their export. The reply encloses the Joint Resolution and an arms-traffic pamphlet.

subfiles.title: Mechanicsburg Woman's Christian Temperance Union protest
subfiles.from: Miss Ehleman, for the Woman's Christian Temperance Union of Mechanicsburg
subfiles.about: Reports a unanimous resolution protesting American provision of war materials to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Mechanicsburg WCTU claims the U.S. supplied half of Japan's raw war materials and frames it as a Christian moral question.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Miss Ehleman
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Responds to the Mechanicsburg union's resolution with the standard Neutrality Act explanation.
subfiles.summary: Yost tells Miss Ehleman a war finding would embargo China and Japan alike, no authority exists to single out Japan, invocation was judged contrary to national interest, and non-arms goods can't be prohibited; totals and pamphlet enclosed.

subfiles.title: Pasadena Presbyterian Church petition addressed directly to Cordell Hull
subfiles.from: Dr. Freeman and members of Pasadena Presbyterian Church
subfiles.about: Petitions for an end to American sales assisting Japanese attacks on Chinese noncombatants.
subfiles.summary: This version of the Pasadena petition is addressed directly to Hull and repeats the charge that American aircraft and munitions supported Japan in an undeclared war. It asks the President to follow the Good Neighbor policy and place morality above profit. The following two pages contain the congregation's signatures.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Dr. Freeman
subfiles.about: Begins the formal reply to the Pasadena petition by explaining the conditions for invoking the Neutrality Act.
subfiles.summary: State acknowledges Dr. Freeman's September 18 petition and begins explaining that Section 1(a) needs a presidential war finding and an embargo would hit both China and Japan; continues past this section.
